message.content: In lions, the most well‑documented dominant genetic trait is the **presence of a mane in adult male lions**. The mane is controlled by a dominant allele (often referred to as “M”) that masks the recessive allele (“m”) which results in a maneless phenotype. Thus, when a male lion inherits at least one copy of the dominant “M” allele, he will develop a mane, whereas only homozygous recessive (mm) individuals remain maneless. This dominant trait is a classic example of how a single allele can dictate a prominent physical characteristic in a species.
